text_translated_detailed:
The King's Pepper and Thin Vessel from Palembang, the 28th of February, 1751. Register of such papers as were sent from here per the King's Pepper and Thin Vessel to Batavia. Consigned to His Excellency, the High and Noble, Strict, and greatly esteemed Lord Jacob Mossel, Governor General, and the Noble and esteemed Lords Councillors of the Netherlands Indies.

No. 1. Original letter to the well-mentioned His High Excellency by the Resident here under today's date directed.

From Palembang, the 28th of February, 1751.

No. 2. Copy letter, from and to as above, dated the 20th of September in the year 1780.

No. 3. Two copies of resolutions dated the 16th of January and the 17th of February, passed here in council, and also given orders to the steersman Abraham Meershoek dated the 16th and 19th of January, filed under letters A and B.

No. 4. [blank]

No. 5. Copy letter from the steersman Meershoek, several times, dated the 22nd of January of the past year, directed to the chief here, resolved, together with a report by the commissioners concerning the aforementioned.

No. 6. From Palembang, the 28th of February, 1751. Incidents concerning Raja Allam handed over to the chief aforementioned, dated the 28th of January and the 2nd of February of this year.

No. 7. The double requisition of necessities for the year 1752/1753, annexed with catalogues of the needed medicines.

No. 8. Two pieces of petitions, at the request to be discharged from the service of the Company and to be placed in citizen freedom by His High Excellency, the High Indian government.

No. 9. Original report by the chief surgeon of this Company concerning the condition of the Company's slaves at Palembang, the 28th of February, 1751, handed over to the chief here.

No. 10. Register of the further business concluded in this post and salary books, together with the annual papers passing through.

Palembang, on the last day of February, 1751. [was signed:] A. A. van Laar, Batavia. To His Excellency,

From Palembang, the 28th of February, 1751.

High and Noble, Strict, greatly esteemed, Earnest, valiant, wise, prudent, and most generous Lord and Lords.

With this glorious and much-desired succession, we felicitate His High Excellency, greatly esteemed, by these means from the depths of our souls. May Jehovah's fiery providence deign to bless the dear person of the well-mentioned His High Excellency, greatly esteemed, with a span of years with perfect health and a fortunate reign, mildly for the welfare of this Dutch company and all its servants. In the month of December, Raja Alang, or so-called King of Siantang, who in the past year had been driven from his unlawful possession by the King of Johor and has since been occupied with murder and piracy around Borneo, Billiton, and hereabouts, came to settle on the island of Banca with 22 vessels and approximately 300 persons strong. From Palembang, the 28th of February, 1751. Of the inhabitants of which, who consist in great part of Siantangers, he immediately knew how to draw a good many to his side, and thus his following grew so much that the same soon found himself very strong there, and consequently too powerful to be driven from there by force by the Palembanger, whose bloody and lascivious nature had been sufficiently known to him from early times. text_translated_detailed: From Palembang, the 28th of February, 1751. Batavia. To His Excellency, the highly esteemed and greatly honored Lord Jacob Mossel, Governor-General, together with the other esteemed and greatly honored gentlemen, counselors of the Netherlands Indies. Highly esteemed, greatly honored, most earnest, manly, wise, prudent, and most generous lord and gentlemen. Meanwhile, departing now under the escort of this vessel from here, toward the King's coast, the first cargo from Palembang on the 20th of February, 1751, consisting of a quantity of 3,440 picols [modern equivalent: approximately 206,400 kg] of thin beancake and 1,300 picols of pepper, namely: per Chialoup [uncertain: vessel type] given by King by Satjo Diprana, 675 picols of thin beancake and 1,000 picols of pepper; per Juragan Jammeljoedin, 375 picols; per Commering, 170 picols and 300 picols; per Roehoe, 950 picols; per Boedin, 600 picols; per Toelejo, 670 picols; these small vessels standing in short order to be followed by many others, after which this dutiful distribution concludes, and with deep respectful obligation I remain, [below which was signed:] Highly esteemed, greatly honored, most earnest, manly, wise, prudent, and most generous lord and gentlemen. text_translated_detailed: From Palembang, the 28th of February, 1751. Your Excellency's greatly honored, entirely obedient and submissive servants. [Was signed:] G. Pan and A. A. van Laar. [In margin:] Palembang, the last of February, 1751. [Below which was signed:] Accorded [was signed:] A. A. van Laar, Batavia. To His Excellency, the highly esteemed, greatly honored Lord Jacob Mossel, Governor-General of the Netherlands Indies. —. Your Excellency, I have with very great sorrow and bitter heartfelt pain learned from the recently received Company's letter, the displeasure of Your Excellency's highly esteemed greatness regarding my conduct toward this king, wherein I in this matter am so fortunate, Your Excellency, highly esteemed greatness, with deep reverence to be able to convince you that during my presence here concerning that prince, I have shown all conceivable friendliness and have never had any disagreement with him, except only over the gross and great neglect of the Contracts to the detriment of my lords and masters, and that I have never, to my knowledge, committed anything improper concerning his highness or given him the slightest legitimate reason for complaint, and that if I had shown somewhat less zeal concerning the true interest of the Company and had not pursued it as a precious pledge, the Sultan would never have invented such accusations against the undersigned, for having to acknowledge that he [with whom one now has a complete friendship] these days himself confessed that previously in this matter he had been greatly misled by his court magnates [the Tormongom Soera Mengala, principal among them, being understood:], by which means those same individuals, through daily practiced machinations, have known how to sow the seeds of hatred and discord against the undersigned in his heart, for which reasons their persons now may not be employed in any matters [concerning this lodge:].

text_translated_detailed: Per the Company's cruiser Pantchiallang Neptunus. From Palembang, the 27th of May 1751. — Batavia. To His Excellency, the highly esteemed and greatly respected Lord Jacob Mossel, Governor-General, together with the further noble and greatly respected gentlemen councillors of the Netherlands Indies. We were honored on the 12th and 14th of this month with Your Excellency's highly esteemed and greatly revered missive of the 17th of December and 20th of April of the past year, together with its enclosures. Excepting the King's letter and the acts of those whose engagement has been elevated, we also remain eager to receive the personnel and personal effects mentioned in the aforesaid missive. From Palembang, the 27th of May 1751. In the meantime, we respectfully proceed to respond and first humbly thank Your Excellency, the highly esteemed and greatly respected Lord, for the great and favorable maintenance toward us, both regarding the disgraceful conduct of Captain Lieutenant Ruts and the resulting poor treatment of this King, as well as for the kind approval concerning certain points of our conduct, while all other commands contained in the aforesaid missive shall be dutifully observed. — Furthermore, it grieves the undersigned in their souls that His Highness, (with whom we now live in such good accord), has again seen fit to come to Your Excellency, the highly esteemed and greatly respected Lord, with a portion of feigned and embellished complaints, troubling us. text_translated_detailed: From Palembang under date 27th May 1751. Translation of Malay letter written by the King of Palembang to their High Excellencies the High Indian Government, received at Batavia on the 29th of July, Year 1751. This letter, which springs from a pure heart, is sent with due high regard by the Padoeka Siri Sultan Ratoe Mahmud Badaruddin, seated upon the Royal throne in the blessed land of Daw at Palembang, addressed to his faithful brother-like and very well-disposed friends, the From Palembang under date 27th of May 1751, Lord Governor-General Jacob Mossel and the assembled Council of India, who are seated in very great power and majesty in the Castle Batavia. text_translated_detailed:
From Banjarmasin on the 14th of May 1751. Batavia. To His High Excellency the High and Esteemed, Most Respected Lord Jacob Mossel, Governor-General and Well-Esteemed Lords Councillors of the Netherlands Indies. High and Esteemed, Strict, Most Respected Lord and Well-Esteemed Lords!

I have had the honor on the 19th of the month of April via Semarang by panjang [a type of boat] under the escort of a sailor and the Chinese merchant Kanjinko to receive your High Excellency's esteemed letters of the 13th of March concerning the Chinese Tsiuw Lak Saij and Tjiuw Goanko, of which at that time not the slightest rumor from Banjarmasin on the 14th of May 1751 could be heard. However, a few days later, on the 28th of April, I was informed that a prau [a type of boat] from the Baviaan with Chinese aboard had landed on Labuan, and the next day came further news that these were indeed the aforementioned Chinese, who had run their vessel aground on the island of Selombo or Pulau Kambing [Kambing Island], and having been stranded, had come over with a passing prau from the Baviaan. Meanwhile, I had the Chaloupe [a type of boat] placed under the command of the free burgher Michiel van der Veer, who, since no other person has been appointed as spy in the Company's service here during this monsoon, I had to retain, and had him depart at night under the pretext of fetching a cargo of sand from Banjarmasin on the 14th of May 1751 to Tobuan, but with orders to Captain-Lieutenant de Jong, who had also gone along, to arrest the Chinese found there immediately upon arrival and to provide them well on his ship, and likewise to keep watch over their accompanying goods. However, since the aforementioned Chinese merchant Ingabei here, on the advice of the Chinese merchant Hanjinko, had also sent a small vessel to fetch those persons, and the Sabandhar [a local official] of Labuan had seized the prau from the Baviaan with its cargo by order of the Ratoe Anum [a local ruler]

text_translated_detailed: the High and Noble Lord Jacob Mossel, first counselor and director general of Dutch India, has entered into the weighty and eminent dignity of Governor General of the Dutch Company. Thus we take the liberty to congratulate His High Excellency with this most distinguished charge in the most respectful manner, under humble wishes and prayers that the Almighty may constantly accompany his high person and all his decisions and undertakings with His precious blessings, and may make his reign a succession of years completely happy for the continuous increase of prestige, splendor, and prosperity of the Company in general, and in particular. From Banjarmasin on the 14th of May 1751. From His High Excellency. — Regarding Your High Excellencies' missive to the Sultan Tondji Dullah, together with the sent gifts addressed to His Highness alone without any missive or gifts for the young prince or Ratoe Anum, I trust that Your High Excellencies will forgive me if I am holding a missive and gifts in abeyance pending further orders, to avoid all suspicion given the present circumstances, especially since both princes, on account of the feared smallpox which has raged so terribly in this kingdom and has not yet ceased, have already withdrawn to the highlands in the past year and still remain there, which is why they cannot now be met with as is customary in the delivery of missives. From Banjarmasin on the 14th of May 1751. And gifts. — In the aforementioned Your High Excellencies' letter of safe conduct I also find mentioned as being forwarded the still-promised 10,000 Spanish reals, but the Lieutenant Kriegsman has let us know that he has no cash on hand, and it also does not appear in the accounts why this is so; therefore I respectfully note this only in hope of clarification, with deep respect. [Undersigned] Your High and Noble, Strict, and Wide-Governing Lord and Well-Noble Gentlemen. [Lower] Your High Excellencies' most obedient and faithful servant. [Was signed] J.

text_translated_detailed: From Banjarmasin on the 22nd of May 1751. Batavia. To His High Excellency the High and Noble, Strict, Wide-Governing Lord Jacob Mossel, Governor General, and Well-Honored Lords, Counselors of Dutch India. Title. On the 6th of December of the previous year I had the honor to receive through the ship the Becarspel Your High Excellencies' esteemed missive of the 10th of August before, accompanied by cash and timber for this Comptoir [Comptoir: trading post], as well as some small items partially requested by the Sultan, all of which has been properly delivered, and with that I take the liberty to express my humble thanks for that shipment. From Banjarmasin on the 22nd of May 1751. Likewise for the permitted write-offs both in the aforementioned Your High Excellency's letters and in subsequent ones of the 9th of January of this year, by which I was honored via Semarang on the 7th of the following month of February. — In view of which last and thereby approved further purchase of gold, which I recently reported on the 14th of this month to Your High Excellencies, I have already made known that in this year we have succeeded considerably better than in the collection of pepper. Therefore, for the Becarspel no cargo is expected to be loaded first, as that vessel is being dispatched via Semarang with the meager quantity of 590 picols [picol: a unit of weight, approximately 133 pounds] of black pepper, which is all that has been delivered since November last. From Banjarmasin on the 22nd of May 1751. Together with 1,001 reals or 616 thalers of gold dust in a sealed copper bowl belonging to Captain Lieutenant Jan de Jong, and the cost of that pepper with the duties amounts to a sum of ƒ12,099.2.–, and the gold Spanish reals 10,472 or 33,510.8. In Banjarmasin on the 29th of September 1751: No. 10. A request for medicines. 11. A notice of unsuitable goods that are now being sent off by the bark. 12. A declaration of these items found short in a package of stockings, etc. At Tatas in the Company's residence on the 29th of September 1751. /was signed:/ J. v. Suchtels /:on the side was noted/ B NB. Moreover, a Malay letter was handed over by Pangerang Maas to their High Excellencies, mentioned B. Batavia E To his High Excellency, the well-esteemed, greatly respected lord Jacob Mossel, Governor General, and further well-esteemed gentlemen counselors of the Netherlands. From Banjarmasin on the 29th of September 1751. High and esteemed, widely commanding lord and well-esteemed gentlemen.

During the night between the 10th and 11th of this month, the first undersigned had the honor to receive, with the arrival of the ship Sijbearspel, your High Excellencies' letters of the 4th of June and 12th of July of this year, and to perceive therein your high favor in his promotion to chief merchant [opperkoopman], for which he takes the liberty to express in all respect hereby his most humble thanks with earnest assurance that he shall not cease to apply himself in all respects to that which your High Excellencies have entrusted to him, and to the advancement of trade here. From Banjarmasin on the 29th of September 1751. It has been serving him for the past year to the utmost painfully, that with regard to the same your High Excellencies have had to communicate various unpleasant tidings, and which still do not appear as favorable as would be wished. For although the pepper this year according to reports has succeeded reasonably well, the fire, by which in the previous year more than 100,000 pepper plants were consumed, has ruined many gardens, and through the severe outbreak of smallpox the remaining ones are in all appearance not maintained as well as would be required.

Translation of a Malay letter written by Ratoe Anoem, son of the Sultan Hamidullah, to His Excellency the High Noble, greatly esteemed Lord Jacob Mossel, Governor General, together with the Noble Lord Council of India, received in Batavia on the 16th of August, Year 1751. Ratoe Anoem, son of the Sultan Hamidullah, expresses his sincere affection, accompanied by endless greetings both by day and by night, because he has received a letter from the Lord from Banjarmasin dated the 29th of July 1752 [note: date discrepancy in original] Governor General Jacob Mossel and the assembled Council of India, who are residing in the Castle of Batavia—. Furthermore, I communicate hereby to the Governor General Jacob Mossel and the assembled Council of India, regarding the request made by Their High Excellencies, I have done my best, but I have not been able to apprehend the same, since such wandering merchants are very scattered everywhere, including among the subjects, for that reason I have given my brother the chief merchant this letter, hoping and trusting that Their High Excellencies will be pleased to pardon me on my behalf, for from Banjarmasin dated the 29th of July 1751, if the Dutch company did not maintain me, I would be subject to great misery, but since the Esteemed Company maintains its residence at Banjar, I lack nothing and everything is in a flourishing condition. —. Furthermore, I request two pieces of small muskets with silver fittings, 10 pounds of gold thread, 10 pounds of silver
